questions.question: A security team must deploy an urgent out-of-band patch today to stop an active exploit on a production server. Which change type fits this request?

options.text: A standard change
An emergency change
A normal change
An unauthorized change

explanation.correct: Change Management supports three ITIL change types: standard, emergency, and normal. An emergency change is a high-priority change implemented immediately to resolve a major incident or apply a security patch. It bypasses group and peer review and goes directly to the Authorize state for CAB approval. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/change-management/change-types.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: A standard change is a pre-authorized, low-risk change that is frequently implemented and has a proven history of success. An urgent, one-off patch for an active exploit does not match that description.
A normal change follows a prescriptive process with two levels of approval before implementation. That is too slow for a patch that must be implemented immediately.
Unauthorized change requests are created when unplanned CI change activity is detected, not raised for a planned urgent fix. The docs list the three change types as standard, emergency, and normal.

source.excerpt: There are three types of changes. When it comes to service changes, a normal change refers to any change that isn't classified as a standard change or an emergency change.

questions.question: A team has a routine TLS certificate renewal with documented steps and a proven success record. Their change manager wants it raised as a standard change rather than a normal change. What key difference supports this?

options.text: Standard changes skip peer review but still require CAB authorization
Standard changes are pre-authorized and skip group, peer, and CAB approval
Standard changes are reserved for urgent fixes that resolve a major incident
Standard changes require two levels of approval before implementation

explanation.correct: Per the Change types page, a standard change is a pre-authorized, low-risk change that is frequently implemented, has repeatable steps and a proven history of success. Because it is pre-approved, it follows a streamlined process without group-level or peer approval and without CAB authorization, whereas a normal change requires assessment, peer or technical approval and CAB authorization. Routine TLS certificate renewals are the docs' own example of a standard change. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/change-management/change-types.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Skipping peer review but still going to the CAB describes an emergency change, which bypasses group and peer review and moves directly to Authorize for CAB approval. Standard changes need no CAB authorization.
Urgent fixes to resolve a major incident or apply a security patch are emergency changes, not standard changes. Standard changes are low-risk, routine, and repeatable.
Two levels of approval (peer or technical approval plus CAB authorization) before implementation is the defining trait of a normal change, not a standard change.

source.excerpt: Changes that are considered standard or pre-approved are commonly put into effect. These changes have a set of established implementation steps and a track record of successful outcomes.

questions.question: A change requester's change request matches the agenda filter criteria of next week's CAB meeting in the CAB workbench. What happens for the requester?

options.text: The request is approved when the meeting starts
The requester is notified of the meeting
The request moves straight to the Scheduled state
The requester must confirm before it is listed

explanation.correct: In the CAB workbench, the CAB manager defines filter criteria that determine which change requests are included in a CAB meeting. If a change request is included in an agenda, the change requester is notified of the CAB meeting in which it is discussed. The requester can attend to present the reasons for the change and explain its intended outcomes and potential risks. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/change-management/cab-workbench.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Being on the agenda does not approve anything. The CAB workbench is used to approve or reject a change request based on the decision taken in the CAB meeting.
A change request moves to the Scheduled state when its approval is granted, not when it is added to a CAB agenda.
Inclusion is driven by the agenda filter criteria. The docs say the requester is notified; they do not need to confirm before the request is listed.

source.excerpt: Such changes require comprehensive assessments and authorizations, including peer or technical approval, Change Management, and change advisory board authorization.

questions.question: An administrator wants conflict detection to flag any change request planned during the year-end code freeze. Which type of schedule should the administrator create for that period?

options.text: A maintenance schedule covering the freeze
A blackout schedule covering the freeze
An information schedule covering the freeze
A CAB meeting schedule covering the freeze

explanation.correct: Blackout schedules specify times during which normal change activity should not be scheduled, and conflict detection raises a conflict when a change request falls inside a blackout window. The Conflict detection page even gives a year-end code freeze as the example use of a blackout schedule. Conflict detection compares a change's CIs and planned dates against blackout and maintenance windows and other active changes. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/change-management/schedule-types-conflict-detection.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: A maintenance schedule defines when changes should be scheduled. Conflict detection flags changes that fall outside a maintenance window, so it would not flag changes inside the freeze.
Information schedules record events such as holidays that teams should know about, but conflict detection does not create conflict records for information schedules.
A CAB meeting schedule in the CAB workbench sets up recurring CAB meetings to review changes. Conflict detection does not evaluate it as a change blackout period.

source.excerpt: The Change Management application helps identify schedule conflicts for change requests by analyzing factors such as configuration items, planned start and end dates, and change scope.

questions.question: A requester asks about a normal change that has received final authorization from Change Management and the CAB. Its planned start date is next week, and no work has started yet. Which state is the change request in?

options.text: Implement
Scheduled
Authorize
Assess

explanation.correct: In the change state model, Scheduled means the change is fully scheduled and authorized and is waiting for its planned start date; an email notification is sent to the requester when the change enters this state. Authorize is the earlier state in which Change Management and the CAB schedule the change and give final authorization, so a change that already has that authorization and is waiting for its window has moved on to Scheduled. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/change-management/c_ChangeStateModel.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Implement is the state in which the planned start date has arrived and the actual implementation work is being carried out. No work has started on this change yet.
Authorize is where Change Management and the CAB schedule the change and provide final authorization. Once that authorization is granted, the change moves on to Scheduled.
Assess is where peer review and technical approval of the change details happen. That step comes before CAB authorization, so this change is past it.

source.excerpt: Authorized means that CAB has provided the final authorization to proceed with the change, and we're simply waiting for the scheduled window.

questions.question: During a major incident, the on-call engineer confirms that restoring service needs an immediate configuration change to a business service. What should the engineer do from the incident record?

options.text: Create a problem record from the incident
Create an emergency change from the incident
Create a service request from the incident
Create a normal change request from the incident

explanation.correct: When the issue behind an incident requires a change to the infrastructure or a business service, a change record is created from the incident. The incident form offers Create Normal, Standard, or Emergency Change. An emergency change is the type implemented immediately to resolve a major incident, and it goes directly to the Authorize state for CAB approval. The Create Emergency Change script copies fields such as short description, description, CI, and priority from the incident. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/incident-management/t_PromoteAnIncident.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: A problem is generated from an incident when the cause is an error or widespread issue. It does not carry out the change needed to restore service.
A request is created from an incident when the resolution for the user is to request hardware or software, not to change a business service.
A normal change needs two levels of approval before implementation. The docs reserve the emergency type for changes implemented immediately to resolve a major incident.

source.excerpt: To be implemented swiftly, emergency changes do not follow the complete lifecycle of a normal change, which can potentially lead to unauthorized changes. To minimize this risk, it is best practice to create emergency changes if they are associated with an incident.

questions.question: A change coordinator adds a change task whose planned start and end dates must fall within the parent change request's planned dates. Which change task type is this?

options.text: Planning type, which prepares the change
Implementation type, which carries it out
Testing type, which verifies the change works
Review type, for post-implementation review

explanation.correct: Change tasks have four types: Planning, Implementation, Testing, and Review. For the Implementation type, which covers tasks that carry out the change, the Planned start date and Planned end date must fall within the planned dates of the change request. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/change-management/create-a-change-task.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Planning tasks plan and prepare the change before implementation. The docs apply the planned-date restriction only to the Implementation type.
Testing tasks verify that the change works as expected. The docs do not apply the planned-date restriction to them.
Review tasks are for post-implementation review. The planned-date restriction applies to Implementation tasks.

source.excerpt: ServiceNow offers four types of change tasks-- namely, planning, implementation, testing, and review tasks.

questions.question: An administrator wants database refresh changes to follow their own set of states, state transitions, and approval policies, with fields pre-filled when the request is created. What should the administrator define?

options.text: A blackout schedule
A new change model
A standard change template
A CAB meeting agenda

explanation.correct: Change models define the process for a specific change use case. They are built from reusable elements such as change states, change state transitions, approval policies, and change templates, and they can show standard field information when a new change request is created with the model. This tailors a fit-for-purpose process for the use case, so a change model meets every requirement in the scenario. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/change-management/manage-change-models.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: A blackout schedule sets times when normal change activity should not be scheduled. Conflict detection uses it, but it does not define states, transitions, or approvals.
A standard change template pre-fills pre-approved values for a standard change from the catalog. It does not define its own set of states, transitions, and approval policies.
A CAB meeting agenda uses filter criteria to pick which change requests a CAB meeting discusses. It does not define the process that a change request follows.

source.excerpt: The process details, such as the specific fields, record states, approvals or pre-approvals, and tasks created are determined by the change model and change policies.

questions.question: A change owner runs Check Conflicts on a change request, and the Conflicts tab shows that the CI is already scheduled by another change during the planned window. What is the documented next step?

options.text: Revert the change to New so that the conflicts are cleared
Review the conflicts and reschedule the change to resolve them
Approve the change so that it skips the conflicting time window
Wait for the conflict status to clear in the Scheduled state

explanation.correct: After running conflict detection manually, the change owner reviews the Conflicts Detected list on the Conflicts tab, which shows the conflict type, such as CI Already Scheduled, and any conflicting change. The documented next step is to resolve the conflicts and reschedule the change. The conflict calendar's Scheduling Assistant can help by offering available time slots that avoid the conflict. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/change-management/t_RunManualConflictDetection.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Revert to New restarts the workflow and cancels pending approvals. It is meant for adding missing CIs before approval and does not resolve a schedule clash.
Approving a change moves it to Scheduled but does not change its planned dates. The CI would still be scheduled by the other change at the same time.
Conflicts are recalculated when the CI, planned dates, or state change. The overlap stays until the schedule changes, so the owner must reschedule rather than wait.

source.excerpt: It is up to the change owner or the assigned to user to review the conflicts and decide whether to amend the change to avoid conflicts or proceed, anyway. We will constantly update the work notes with the justification if conflicts are ignored.

questions.question: An administrator documents how the risk of a change request can be calculated in Change Management. Which two methods do the docs describe? (Choose two.)

options.text: Risk Calculator rules on predefined conditions
CAB members voting on risk during a meeting
Risk assessment answers given by the end user
Conflict detection results for the planned dates

explanation.correct: There are two methods to calculate the risk of a change. The Change Risk Calculator, active in the base system by default, uses predefined properties and conditions to calculate a risk value. Change Management - Risk Assessment, which is optional, uses information provided by the end user to assess a risk value. The two can be used individually or together. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/change-management/c_RskAsmtCalc.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The docs name only the Risk Calculator and Risk Assessment as risk calculation methods. CAB meetings review and authorize change requests; they are not a risk calculation method.
Conflict detection helps you schedule change requests for the least impact to stakeholders. It is described separately from risk assessment and calculation and does not set the risk value.

source.excerpt: To determine the risk of a change, there are two methods available. The first is through risk conditions, which utilize predefined properties and conditions to calculate a risk value. The second is through risk assessments, which rely on the information provided by the end user to assess a risk value.

questions.question: A developer marked the 'Patch Fixes' update set as Complete, then found two more fixes that must go to the same target instance. What do the docs recommend?

options.text: Set it back to In progress and add the fixes
Create another update set and commit both in order
Delete the completed set and rebuild all changes
Keep working, since Complete sets still track changes

explanation.correct: Once an update set is complete, do not change it back to In progress. Instead, create another update set for the rest of the changes and commit them in the order they were created. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/application-development/system-update-sets/t_CompleteUpdateSets.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The docs say that once an update set is complete, you should not change it back to In progress.
To revert a customization, the docs say to back out the update set rather than delete it. An update set can be deleted only when it contains no sys_update_xml entries.
After an update set is marked Complete, additional customizations aren't tracked in it.

questions.question: A security administrator notices that the glide.installation.production property is set to false on the company's production instance. What is the documented effect?

options.text: It is still handled as production, so nothing changes
It is handled as non-production, permitting zboot
It affects functional behavior, not security
It is expected, as the property's default is false

explanation.correct: If glide.installation.production is not set to the recommended value of true, the instance is not treated as a production instance, permitting zboot and other potentially dangerous scripts. The docs say to set the property to true on a production instance, because allowing a production instance to be evaluated as non-production can lead to information disclosure or denial of service. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-security/instance-security-hardening-settings/sc-production-instance-behavior.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The docs say an instance with this property not set to true is not treated as a production instance.
The docs rate the setting as a security risk (severity 6.3, CVSS Medium) and list its functional impact as None.
The docs list the default value of glide.installation.production as true, and the recommended value is also true. A value of false is not the default.

questions.question: A small company runs its service desk as a tenant on a service provider's domain-separated instance shared with other customers. Which statement describes this multiple-tenant setup?

options.text: The company decides when the instance is upgraded
The provider decides when to upgrade and add services
The company has higher upfront costs than a single tenant
The company must hire staff to administer the instance

explanation.correct: A multi-tenant architecture is a single instance serving multiple tenants. On a multiple-tenant instance, someone else owns the instance, possibly a service provider with multiple customers. They upgrade when they want and put new services on the instance when they want, and a centralized staff administers configurations, integrations, and upgrades. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-security/bp-dom-sep-how-it-works.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Choosing your own upgrade timing describes a single-tenant instance: 'You can upgrade when you want.'
Domain tenants have lower upfront costs. Higher upfront costs and administrative overhead are listed for a single-tenant instance.
Domain tenants do not have to employ a staff to administer the environment, because a centralized staff does this.

course.lessonTitle: Explore the power of the ServiceNow Platform

questions.question: A CAB manager wants to set up a recurring weekly CAB meeting, define its attendees, and use filter criteria to pick which change requests go on each agenda. Which feature should the manager use?

options.text: The standard change catalog
The CAB workbench
The conflict calendar
Change approval policies

explanation.correct: The CAB workbench lets a CAB manager schedule, plan, and manage CAB meetings. It can define a recurring meeting schedule and the attendees for each occurrence, and it uses filter criteria to decide which change requests go on a meeting's agenda. It also provides a change calendar, lets attendees approve or reject changes based on CAB decisions, and records meeting notes. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/change-management/cab-workbench.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The standard change catalog lists pre-approved standard change templates that users can request. It does not schedule CAB meetings or build their agendas.
The conflict calendar shows the scheduling conflicts for one change request and offers the Scheduling Assistant. It does not manage CAB meetings or their attendees.
Change approval policies generate approvals by evaluating decisions and approval definitions. They do not schedule recurring CAB meetings or set agendas.

questions.question: An administrator merges three update sets from the same application, and two of them contain changes to the same business rule. What does the merge do with that business rule?

options.text: It blocks the merge until the overlap is resolved
It moves the most recent change into the new set
It asks the administrator which version to keep
It combines both versions into one merged record

explanation.correct: When you merge update sets, the most recent change for each object is moved from the original sets to the new set, and changes that aren't merged remain in the original sets. The system decides which record is most recent by comparing the Updated field of the records, not the sys_updated_on value in the payload. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/application-development/system-update-sets/t_MergeUpdateSets.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The documented procedure is to select Merge and confirm. The most recent change for each object is then moved, and a message shows how many updates were moved and how many were skipped.
The system chooses the most recent record itself by comparing the Updated field. The administrator then checks the original sets to verify that the correct changes were moved.
Only the most recent change for each object moves to the new set. Older changes are not combined; they remain in the original sets.

questions.question: During the Implement state of a normal change, the implementer hits a critical issue and backs out the work, so the change cannot be completed as planned. How should this outcome be recorded?

options.text: Move it to Review and record the outcome in the close code and notes
Use Revert to New so that the change can be resubmitted for approval
Close it with a successful close code so the change metrics stay clean
Change its type to Emergency and send it on to the CAB for approval

explanation.correct: After implementation work ends, the change moves to the Review state. In Review, the change requester decides whether the change was successful, and a post-implementation review can be held. To close the change, the user enters a Close code and Close notes in the Closure Information section, which records the actual outcome. A change cannot be canceled once it is in Review. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/change-management/c_ChangeStateModel.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Revert to New is used for Normal changes in Assess or Emergency changes in Authorize when CIs were missed before approval. It does not record a failed implementation.
In Review, the requester determines whether the change was successful. Recording a failed change as successful would make the closure information inaccurate.
A change's Type can be changed only while it is in the New state and before any approvals exist, so a change in Implement cannot be converted to Emergency.

questions.question: A new team member asks what role the Change Advisory Board (CAB) plays in the ServiceNow change process. Which answer is accurate?

options.text: It authorizes normal and emergency changes before implementation
It implements approved changes on behalf of the change owner
It pre-approves each standard change request when it is submitted
It runs conflict detection on every change in the Scheduled state

explanation.correct: According to the Change types page, normal changes need peer or technical approval and CAB authorization before implementation. Emergency changes skip group and peer review and go directly to the Authorize state for CAB approval. CAB meetings are typically used to review and authorize change requests and to review recently implemented changes, so the CAB is an authorization body, not an implementation team. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/change-management/change-types.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The CAB reviews and authorizes changes. The actual work is done by the implementer during the Implement state, not by the CAB.
Standard changes are already pre-authorized and need no CAB authorization. Requests created from the catalog skip the Assess and Authorize states.
Conflict detection runs automatically when CIs or planned dates are entered or changed, or it is run manually from the change. It is not a CAB task.

questions.question: Two teams have planned changes on the same server CI for overlapping time windows. The change manager wants this flagged automatically when the CI or planned dates are entered. Which feature does this?

options.text: Change conflict detection
A UI policy on the change form
The change risk calculator
A change approval policy

explanation.correct: Conflict detection identifies scheduling conflicts from a change's configuration items and planned start and end dates. One reason it flags a conflict is that the CI is already scheduled at the given date and time. It can run automatically when the Configuration item or planned start and end dates are entered or updated, and the results appear in the Conflicts section of the change request. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/change-management/c_ConflictDetection.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: UI policies change form behavior, such as making fields mandatory, read-only, or hidden. They do not compare one change's schedule against other changes on the same CI.
The change risk calculator calculates the risk and impact of a change from defined rules. It does not detect overlapping schedules between changes on the same CI.
Change approval policies generate approvals from decision conditions. They decide who approves a change, not whether its window overlaps another change on the CI.

questions.question: A network team wants its routine switch firmware procedure offered in the standard change catalog. How does a change become available in that catalog?

options.text: It is added as an ordinary service catalog item
Its template is proposed and then approved
It completes one successful normal change first
It is submitted as an emergency change for the CAB

explanation.correct: The standard change catalog contains the changes that Change Management has approved as standard changes. Change Management uses a proposal process to control which changes become available in the catalog, and the catalog lets you request, review, and approve standard change templates. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/change-management/c_StandardChangeCatalogPlugin.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Standard changes are offered through standard change templates. A proposal process controls which changes become available in the standard change catalog.
The docs do not make a change standard after one successful normal change. Inclusion in the catalog is controlled by the proposal process.
An emergency change is for a high-priority change implemented immediately, such as a fix for a major incident. It is not the route for adding a template to the standard change catalog.

questions.question: A vendor will perform a platform upgrade that it controls, and the change manager only needs to record the change, with no approval workflow. Which change model fits this?

options.text: Normal change model
Emergency change model
Change Registration model
Unauthorized change model

explanation.correct: Change Registration captures changes controlled by external teams or vendors, such as platform upgrades or vendor-managed changes, and the model has no approval workflow. Its configuration covers who can register external changes and who is notified when one is registered. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/configure-change-registration-model-scm.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Normal change requests follow a prescriptive process that requires two levels of approval before implementation.
The Emergency model has an Authorize state, a business approval gate with approvers configured for each risk level.
An emergency unauthorized change request is created automatically when Service Mapping detects unauthorized change activity on a CI. It is not used to record a planned vendor change.

source.excerpt: In an out-of-the-box installation, there are several examples available, such as the Change Registration model, which records change requests from an external system without any associated approvals.

questions.question: During a CAB meeting, the CAB manager works in the CAB workbench. Which two tasks does the CAB workbench support? (Choose two.)

options.text: Approve or reject a change request
Hide agenda items from the change requesters
Record and share the meeting notes
Approve agenda changes before the meeting starts

explanation.correct: The CAB workbench helps manage CAB meetings. Among other things, you can approve or reject a change request based on the decision taken in the CAB meeting, and you can record meeting notes from a specific CAB meeting and share them with the other attendees. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/change-management/cab-workbench.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The workbench does the opposite: if a change request is included in an agenda, the change requester is notified of the CAB meeting in which it is discussed, and can attend to present the change.
The workbench is used to approve or reject a change request based on the decision taken in the CAB meeting, not ahead of the meeting.

source.excerpt: The CAB Workbench can schedule in-person meetings and conference calls.

questions.question: A change manager has both the Change Risk Calculator and Change Management - Risk Assessment active. For one change request, the calculator returns Moderate and the assessment returns High. Which risk value is selected?

options.text: Moderate, the Risk Calculator result
High, the higher of the two results
Moderate, the lower of the two results
High, since the assessment takes priority

explanation.correct: The two risk methods can be used individually or together. If they are used together, the highest risk value from both methods is always selected, so High is used here. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/change-management/c_RskAsmtCalc.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The Risk Calculator result does not take priority. When both methods are used, the highest value from both is selected.
The docs say the highest risk value is selected, not the lowest.
High is selected because it is the higher value, not because the assessment takes priority. If the calculator returned the higher value, that value would be used.

source.excerpt: To determine the risk of a change, there are two methods available. The first is through risk conditions, which utilize predefined properties and conditions to calculate a risk value. The second is through risk assessments, which rely on the information provided by the end user to assess a risk value.

questions.question: Implementation work on a normal change is finished and the change is now in the Review state. A manager then asks the change owner to cancel the change request. What happens?

options.text: It is canceled and the reason goes to work notes
Cancel isn't available while it is in Review
It must be reverted to New and then canceled
It can be canceled once the close code is set

explanation.correct: The Cancel option for a change request in the Review state is disabled. This prevents cancelling the request when the work is complete and waiting for review. A change can be canceled at any point when it is no longer required, except from a Closed state. You cannot cancel a change request in the Review state. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/change-management/c_ChangeStateModel.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: This is how Cancel Change works in states where it is allowed: the reason is added to the Work Notes field. In the Review state, the Cancel option is disabled.
Revert to New moves a normal change from the Assess state, or an emergency change from Authorize, back to New. It is not available from Review.
The close code and close notes are entered to close the change request. Cancel remains disabled in the Review state.

source.excerpt: Once the change is implemented, this tab will automatically update with the actual start and end date.

questions.question: An emergency change request is rejected because the approvers decide it should have been a normal change. What can the requester now do?

options.text: Nothing; it is closed and a new request is needed
Change its type to Normal and resubmit it
Wait in Authorize for the CAB to reverse it
Use Revert to New from the Review state

explanation.correct: If a normal or emergency change request is rejected, its state is set to New. Because it is in New, the type can be changed again. For example, if an emergency change is rejected because it should be normal, you can change the Type to Normal and resubmit the change request. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/change-management/c_ChangeStateModel.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: A rejected change request goes to the New state, not Closed, so the same record can be edited and resubmitted.
Rejection moves the change request to the New state. It does not stay in Authorize.
Revert to New is used from Assess (normal) or Authorize (emergency) when approval has been requested. A rejected change is already in New.

source.excerpt: If the change is rejected, comments are necessary to explain why, and the change is reverted to its new state.

questions.question: In Service Operations Workspace, a CAB manager sets up a CAB definition for a board that will review only emergency changes. Which field sets this?

options.text: The Rolling Meeting Window field
The CAB Type field set to Emergency
The Complete Preapproved Changes option
The Notification lead time field

explanation.correct: On the CAB Definition form, the CAB Type field sets the type of CAB meeting the definition is used for: Normal or Emergency. The CAB type determines the urgency and the required level of scrutiny for the change. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/service-operations-workspace/cm-create-cab-definition-sow.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Rolling Meeting Window is the number of days for which CAB meetings are created.
Complete Preapproved Changes marks pre-approved change requests as Complete in the CAB meeting agenda so that approvers do not have to review them.
Notification lead time is the advance notification about agenda items to be discussed. It does not set the board type.

source.excerpt: The Emergency Change Advisory Board, ECAB, is a subset of the CAB responsible for handling emergency changes. Unlike the CAB, the ECAB operates under stricter timelines and focuses primarily on minimizing potential risks.

questions.question: A change manager knows conflict detection flags a CI that is already booked by another change. Which two other situations are documented conflict reasons? (Choose two.)

options.text: The CI's assignee is booked at that same time
A child CI is outside every blackout window
A parent CI is outside its maintenance window
The CI is inside its defined maintenance window

explanation.correct: Conflict detection identifies conflicts for several reasons, including when the CI is assigned to a person already scheduled at the given date and time, and when a parent or child of the CI is not in the maintenance window. Other reasons are a CI or its parent or child already being scheduled, or being in a blackout window. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/change-management/c_ConflictDetection.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The documented reason is that the CI, or a parent or child of the CI, is in a blackout window. Being outside blackout windows is not a conflict.
The documented reason is that the CI is not in the maintenance window. A CI inside its maintenance window is not a conflict.

source.excerpt: These conflicts may arise if the CIs are already scheduled at the given date and time, if a parent or child of the configuration item is already scheduled, or if the configuration item parent or child falls outside the maintenance window. Perhaps the configuration item, its parent, or its child may be within a blackout window.

questions.question: With ITSM Roles - Change Management active, an auditor must view all change requests and the CAB workbench without being able to edit change records. Which role fits best?

options.text: sn_change_write
sn_change_read
sn_change_admin
sn_incident_read

explanation.correct: The Change read [sn_change_read] role gives read access to the Change Management application and related records. A user with sn_change_read can view all change requests as well as the CAB workbench. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/change-management/installed-with-cm-itsm-roles.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Change write [sn_change_write] gives write access to Change Management records, which is more than the auditor should have.
Change admin [sn_change_admin] gives configuration and authorization access for Change Management system properties and contains sn_change_write.
sn_incident_read gives read access to Incident Management records and the major incident workbench, not to change requests.

source.excerpt: The ITIL role is crucial for anyone in a support group responsible for implementing changes. This role enables users to create, update, and close change and configuration items.
